summary: Specifies Flexible Algorithm, which lets IS-IS and OSPF compute paths using operator-defined metrics and constraints rather than only the default IGP metric. It also describes how Segment Routing prefix segments can be used with these algorithms to steer traffic along the resulting paths.

eli5.summary: Normally a map app finds the shortest route. Flexible Algorithm lets the network choose other goals too, like the fastest road or one that avoids certain towns.

questions: how to do constraint-based routing in ospf or is-is
how does flex-algo choose a winning definition
what is the flex-algorithm number range
subtitle: Let IS-IS and OSPF compute their own constrained paths, such as lowest delay or avoiding certain links, without separate tunnels.

tldr.problem: IGPs normally compute paths only from the IGP metric, so networks that need different metrics or constraints have used RSVP-TE or SR-TE tunnels to steer traffic elsewhere.
tldr.mechanism: Routers advertise a Flexible Algorithm Definition (calculation-type, metric-type and constraints) tied to a number from 128 to 255. Each router that participates computes paths for that number, and Segment Routing Prefix-SIDs or SRv6 locators carry traffic along them.
tldr.outcome: The IGP itself computes constraint-based paths. RFC 9350 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9843 and RFC 9917.

today: RFC 9350 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 9843 and RFC 9917, so read those with it.

sections.title: Why Flexible Algorithm Exists
sections.content:
An IGP path based on the shortest IGP metric is often replaced by a traffic-engineered path, because the metric does not reflect every requirement. For example, if the metric reflects bandwidth but the user's traffic is delay sensitive, the best IGP path may not be the best path for that user.

Networks have used RSVP-TE and SR-TE for this, where a separate TE component computes paths from other metrics or constraints, often represented as tunnels. RFC 9350 instead extends IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 so that routers can advertise a calculation-type, a metric-type and a set of topology constraints. A given combination is a Flexible Algorithm Definition (FAD), and the router assigns it a Flex-Algorithm value.

The RFC also describes how SR-MPLS Prefix-SIDs and SRv6 locators can be associated with a Flex-Algorithm, so each one represents a path computed by that algorithm.
sections.eli5: Instead of building special side roads for each need, the whole road network learns several ways of choosing routes, such as fastest or avoiding bad neighborhoods.

sections.title: Definitions and Flex-Algorithm Numbers
sections.content:
A Flexible Algorithm Definition is the set of (a) a calculation-type, (b) a metric-type and (c) a set of constraints. A Flex-Algorithm is a numeric identifier in the range 128 to 255 that configuration associates with a FAD. These values come from the IANA "IGP Algorithm Types" registry.

The meaning of each number is defined by the operator. As long as all routers in the domain agree on what a number represents, the computation is consistent and traffic is not subject to looping. Possible constraints include using a particular plane of the network, an extended metric, or including or avoiding links with specific affinities.

Not every router has to take part. Participation in a Flex-Algorithm is set by configuration, and only a subset of the participating routers need to advertise the definition.
sections.eli5: Each Flex-Algorithm number is a recipe name. Everyone must agree what the recipe called 130 means, otherwise the routes would not match up.

sections.title: Advertising the Definition
sections.content:
In IS-IS the FAD is a sub-TLV (type 26) of the Router CAPABILITY TLV 242. In OSPF it is a top-level TLV (type 16) of the Router Information LSA, and OSPF requires area-scoped flooding for it. Both carry the same fixed fields: Flex-Algorithm (128 to 255), Metric-Type, Calc-Type and Priority (0 to 255, higher is preferred), followed by optional sub-TLVs.

The defined metric-types are 0 (the IGP metric), 1 (minimum unidirectional link delay) and 2 (the TE metric). Calc-Type uses a value from 0 to 127 from the IGP Algorithm Types registry, and 0 means Shortest Path First.

Constraints are sub-TLVs: exclude admin group, include-any admin group, include-all admin group, and exclude SRLG. A flags sub-TLV carries the M-flag, and separate prefix metric sub-TLVs carry Flex-Algorithm-specific prefix metrics. Link attributes used by Flex-Algorithm must be advertised with Application-Specific Link Attribute (ASLA) advertisements, using a new Flexible Algorithm application bit (bit 3, the X-bit), unless the IS-IS L-flag requires legacy advertisements.
sections.eli5: A router posts a notice saying: recipe 130 means use the delay numbers, skip the red roads, and here is how important my notice is.

sections.title: Choosing the Winning Definition
sections.content:
All routers that participate in a Flex-Algorithm and share an advertisement scope MUST agree on its definition, or loop-free forwarding cannot be guaranteed. Different routers may advertise different definitions, so each participating router applies two ordered rules.

  1. Among the FADs advertised in the area, including its own, pick those with the numerically greatest priority.
  2. If several tie, pick the one from the router with the numerically greatest System-ID (IS-IS) or Router ID (OSPF).

The result is the winning FAD. If a node is configured to participate but has no valid FAD, or the winning FAD uses a calculation-type, metric-type, constraint, flag or sub-TLV it does not support, it MUST stop participating. It then must not announce participation and must remove the related forwarding state. A router that is not configured to participate MUST ignore FADs for that algorithm, though it MAY still advertise one.

Any change to a FAD may briefly disrupt traffic, similar to any event that needs network-wide convergence.
sections.eli5: If two notices disagree, the one marked most important wins. If they are equally important, the one from the router with the bigger ID wins, so everybody picks the same one.

sections.title: Computing the Paths
sections.content:
A router must be configured to participate and must have selected the FAD before it computes anything. Participation is advertised per data plane, and the computation uses the winning FAD's metric-type and calculation-type. Segment Routing data planes (SR-MPLS and SRv6) MUST prune nodes that do not advertise participation.

Links are then pruned in this order:

  1. Remove a link if it has any color in the exclude admin group rule.
  2. Remove it if it belongs to any SRLG in the exclude SRLG rule.
  3. With an include-any rule, remove it if it has none of the listed colors.
  4. With an include-all rule, remove it if it lacks any of the listed colors.
  5. If the FAD uses a metric other than the IGP metric and the link does not advertise it, remove the link. A metric of 0 MUST NOT be assumed.

A computation is limited to a single area, so the path to an inter-area or inter-domain prefix is computed to the egress ABR or ASBR, which handles the next area. With the M-flag set, Flex-Algorithm prefix metrics are advertised between areas so the end-to-end choice can be better. Without it, using Flex-Algorithm for inter-area prefixes is NOT RECOMMENDED because traffic may loop or be persistently dropped.
sections.eli5: First the router crosses out the roads it must not use, step by step. Then it finds the best route on what is left, using the chosen kind of distance.

sections.title: Forwarding Traffic
sections.content:
In SR-MPLS, a Prefix-SID advertisement includes an algorithm value. When that value is a Flex-Algorithm, the Prefix-SID is tied to paths computed by it, and the path is installed using the MPLS label for that Prefix-SID. If there is no such path, traffic meant for it MUST be dropped rather than sent elsewhere.

In SRv6, each node has a locator for every topology and algorithm pair it supports, and the locator carries the algorithm value. Paths to a locator with a Flex-Algorithm value MUST be computed with that algorithm, and forwarding entries for algorithms the node does not participate in MUST NOT be installed.

Loop Free Alternate (LFA) backup paths for a Flex-Algorithm MUST use the same constraints as the primary paths and only SIDs advertised for that algorithm. Other data planes must define their own Flex-Algorithm forwarding, which is outside this RFC.
sections.eli5: Each special route gets its own road sign. If no road exists for that sign, the traffic stops instead of taking a wrong road.

sections.title: Operating Flex-Algorithms
sections.content:
The scope of both the computation and the FAD is an area. The FAD for a number does not have to be identical in every area, so one number could minimize delay in one area and favor bandwidth in another. IS-IS allows an L1/L2 router to regenerate the winning FAD from level 2 into level 1, but never from level 1 into level 2. In OSPF, the AS flooding scope of the RI LSA can spread a FAD across the domain.

A link can be made a last resort by setting its delay value to 16,777,215 (2^24 - 1), or made unreachable for those algorithms by removing the ASLA advertisement. Changing a FAD may force network-wide SPF recomputation, so changes should be planned. The 128 to 255 range allows many algorithms, but typically only a limited subset is expected to be deployed.

The extension adds no new backward-compatibility issues, because IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 already handle unrecognized TLVs and sub-TLVs.
sections.eli5: Different towns can use the same recipe name for different goals. Changing a recipe means everyone has to recalculate, so do it carefully.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names two new ways to disrupt IGP networks. An attacker can hijack a Flex-Algorithm by advertising a FAD with priority 255 or any priority higher than the legitimate nodes. An attacker could also make a router look as if it supports a Flex-Algorithm when it does not, or the reverse.

Existing IGP authentication extensions can address both: RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 for IS-IS, RFC 2328 and RFC 7474 for OSPFv2, and RFC 4552 and RFC 5340 for OSPFv3. If an authenticated node is taken over, it can advertise any FAD, for example with an unsupported metric-type, and cause traffic to be misrouted or lost. Authentication cannot prevent this, and it is no different from advertising any other incorrect information through IS-IS or OSPF.
sections.eli5: A trickster could post a fake notice marked extra important. Passwords on the notice board help, but a trusted router that goes bad can still post bad notices.
